# Parsimony (Occam's razor) (`occams_razor`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by formal_logic
- Core idea: Of two explanations that account for the same observations equally well, prefer the one that assumes fewer separate things, and do not add an entity or cause unless the evidence forces it. The reason is practical: every added assumption is another way of being wrong and makes the explanation harder to test, while a story with enough spare parts can fit anything. It is a rule for choosing what to test first, not a proof that the world is simple. Newton's version: admit no more causes than are true and sufficient to explain the appearances.
- Pitfalls:
  - Misquoting it as 'the simplest explanation is usually true'; it only compares explanations that fit the facts equally well
  - Attributing 'entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity' to Ockham; that wording is John Punch's of 1639, and the name 'Occam's razor' dates from 1852
  - Claiming Copernicus won because his system was simpler; it still needed about as many circles as Ptolemy's until Kepler's ellipses
  - Using it against God or spirits in front of theologians; Ockham himself used it within theology and exempted revealed truths
- History: greece: c. 350 BC – Aristotle: the demonstration from fewer postulates is superior (Posterior Analytics I.25); c. 150 AD Ptolemy prefers the simplest hypothesis that saves the phenomena; india: classical period – 'lightness' (laghava) of assumptions as a standard argument in Nyaya and Mimamsa debate; europe: c. 1320 – William of Ockham: 'plurality is never to be posited without necessity'; 1687 Newton's first rule of reasoning; 1852 the phrase 'Occam's razor' (William Hamilton)
- Read:
  - William of Ockham, Summa logicae (c. 1323)
  - Elliott Sober, Ockham's Razors: A User's Manual (2015)
